items.title: US economy roars ahead in third quarter, inflation remains high in October By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027. The sharp upward revision to gross domestic product last quarter, reported by the Commerce Department on Wednesday, marked the quickest economic growth pace in three years. It reflected upgrades to consumer spending and business investment, mostly related to artificial intelligence. Robust domestic demand is fueling inflation, with a measure of underlying price pressures in October posting its biggest year-over-year increase since late 2023. The economy has powered ahead despite the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran. "It is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "It was once thought that import tariffs and energy prices from the Mideast war were one-off factors behind the higher inflation numbers, but increasingly the inflation fires look to be stoked by old-fashioned economic demand pressures." GDP increased at a 4.3% annualized rate last quarter, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its second estimate of third-quarter GDP. It was the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2023. The economy was previously estimated to have grown at a 3.4% pace. Economists polled by Reuters had expected GDP growth to be revised up to a 3.5% pace. The economy grew at a 2.2% rate in the April-June quarter. Growth in consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, was revised up to a 4.2% rate. That was the strongest pace since the fourth quarter of 2024 and was an upgrade from the previously reported 3.8% pace. Spending is being driven mostly by higher-income households, whose wealth was boosted by the stock market before the ongoing AI-led selloff. Economists expect consumer spending to slow to a still-healthy pace in the fourth quarter, though declining gasoline prices should ease some of the financial pressure on middle- and lower-income households. Average retail gasoline prices have dropped below $4 a gallon for the first time since mid-July, data from the US Energy Information Administration showed. Disposable household income, adjusted for taxes and inflation, rebounded in October, and the saving rate increased after declining for two straight months, the BEA said in another report. Low layoffs, with first-time claims for state unemployment benefits at a 57-year low, are also expected to help underpin spending. But some of the relief at the gasoline pump could be offset by higher prices elsewhere after President Donald Trump on Wednesday fired a new tariff salvo against 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union. ... The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index increased 0.3% in October after gaining 0.5% in September, the BEA said. PCE inflation was lifted by higher prices for goods, including food and household furnishings, as well as services such as recreation, dining out and hotel stays. In the 12 months through October, PCE inflation increased 3.8% after advancing 3.6% in September. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the PCE Price Index increased 0.3% for the third straight month. So-called core PCE inflation increased 3.3% on a year-over-year basis in October, the largest advance since November 2023, after climbing 3.1% in September. The Fed tracks the PCE price measures for its 2% inflation target. Financial markets have priced in a quarter-percentage-point rate hike at the US central bank’s December 8-9 meeting from the current 3.75%-4.00% range, and are expecting another increase in January, CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has signaled he could support a bigger half-percentage-point rate increase to quell inflation. Economists, however, said tightening financial market conditions amid an equities selloff had reduced the need for such an aggressive move.

items.title: A realignment of US politics? What Democrats’ midterm blowout really means. - CSMonitor.com
items.excerpt: The numbers are staggering. Come January, Democrats will have substantial majorities in both houses of Congress – a return from the political wilderness unlike any seen in the United States in decades. Republicans have reacted to the midterm blowout with a mix of recriminations and resolve, some blaming an unpopular President Donald Trump, and many pledging to do the hard work of winning back voters’ trust in 2028. And Democrats, still basking in the larger-than-expected blue wave, are looking ahead to the new year with both excitement and trepidation. Their 56-44 Senate majority and 259-173 advantage in the House (with three races still undecided) mean plenty of opportunity to show voters what they stand for. It’s the largest House majority for either party in three decades and, in the nationwide vote count for House seats, the biggest margin of victory (14%) since 1974. Democrats face the challenge of governing with a defiant Republican president, whose new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, has signaled plans to bypass Congress with aggressive use of executive authority. But it’s a new day for the party, which will soon enjoy all the constitutional powers that come with running the legislative branch. To some prominent Democrats, the 2026 results point to nothing less than a recasting of the electoral landscape after losing the “trifecta” – House, Senate, and White House – in 2024. “This is a realignment,” Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, seen as a potential presidential candidate in 2028, told reporters after the midterms. Others aren’t so sure. What happened on Nov. 3, they say, was not a permanent shift in allegiance toward Democrats but a referendum on President Trump – and a cry of frustration over the cost of living, the Iran war, the harsh treatment of immigrants, and perceived corruption. Those top issues combined to produce a big leftward swing among some groups that had, just two years earlier, moved toward Mr. Trump’s Republican Party: young people, Hispanic voters, and Black voters. “We tried to talk about a realignment after the last presidential race” – and look what happened, says Amy Dacey, head of the Sine Institute for Policy and Politics at American University and a former executive director of the Democratic National Committee. If anything, this year’s election is “a reminder that no political coalition is permanent, and no party can take its voters for granted.”

Now, it's set to take place Saturday. The parade will feature the same balloons, floats, and 1,000 clowns, with added performances by LL Cool J and Gloria Gaynor. Will Coss, Macy’s Studios vice president, says the team quickly adjusted plans to deliver the event. The storm forced the first-ever postponement, leaving performers scrambling to extend their stays. Most bands and performers managed to adjust their schedules. NBC will broadcast the parade, and the weather is expected to be dry with manageable winds. It is a companion piece to 2023's “i/o,” transforming the collection into 25 tracks. Gabriel shared his thoughts in a London-based interview with The Associated Press' Hilary Fox. He discussed the symbolism of full moons, artificial intelligence's impact and the role of activism in music. He believes AI can democratize creativity but acknowledges it could lead to job losses. Gabriel also touched on the importance of speaking out for causes and reflected on his time with Genesis. He attended their final show in London, finding it an emotional and significant moment. Relocated to a Russian town where the government is conscripting men into the Ukraine war, it follows Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) as he discovers his wife is having an affair. Focker- in-Law Out now Robert De Niro, Ben Stiller and Teri Polo reprise their roles in the Focker franchise, while Ariana Grande plays the new fiancee to Pam and Greg’s beloved son Henry Focker. Per franchise lore, the interloper must be put through her paces to ensure she is worthy of a place in the circle of trust. items.title: What To Watch On TV And Streaming Saturday, November 28, 2026
items.excerpt: On TV this Saturday: The delayed Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade airs on NBC, Lacey Chabert visits Disney World in her new Hallmark movie, and Claire Foy and Andrew Garfield's "The Magic Faraway Tree" hits HBO proper. ## Showtimes for November 28, 2026 8:30 AM ET ### Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade NBC Natasha Bedingfield, Baha Men, Blues Traveler, DEVO, Jimmy Fallon and The Roots, Feid, EJAE, Mckenna Grace, Indigo Girls, Icona Pop, JoJo, Wyclef Jean, Queen Latifah, Il Volo, Natalie Merchant, Jamie Miller, Ryan Peter Murphy, Leslie Odom Jr., Keke Palmer, Anthony Ramos, RAYE, RIIZE, and Smash Mouth perform; Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb, and Al Roker host. 6:00 PM ET ### The Most Wonderful Secret Hallmark Channel MOVIE PREMIERE A burned-out art teacher (Tammin Sursok) is chosen for a small town's Christmas scavenger hunt and enlists her electrician neighbor (Peter Porte) to help revive its holiday block party, sparking both her passion for teaching and feelings for him. 8:00 PM ET ### A Christmas Rescue Great American Family MOVIE PREMIERE When a devoted doctor and a visiting veterinarian team up for a Christmas pet adoption event, their shared mission to find homes for rescue animals may lead them to a home for their own hearts as well; Trevor Donovan and Stephanie Bennett star. ### Christmas Everyday: Married and Bright Lifetime MOVIE PREMIERE Chicago fashion designer Fancy (Brandy Norwood) plans her dream Christmas wedding while juggling mounting business pressures and the return of an ex, threatening her future with fiancé Jaylen (Robert C. Riley); Debbi Morgan and Sy'Rai Smith co-star. ### Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True Hallmark Channel MOVIE PREMIERE A woman (Lacey Chabert) spends Christmas at Walt Disney World with her family, only to discover that a disastrous recent first date (Travis Van Winkle) is staying next door; Richard Kind and Christy Carlson Romano co-star. ### The Magic Faraway Tree Polly (Claire Foy), Tim (Andrew Garfield), and their three children are forced to relocate to the remote English countryside where the children discover a magical tree that can transport them to fantastical lands.

Postponed Macy's 100th Thanksgiving parade mostly the same, but now with LL Cool J and Gloria Gaynor NEW YORK (AP) — Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed due to a storm for the first time in its history. Now, it's set to take place Saturday. The parade will feature the same balloons, floats, and 1,000 clowns, with added performances by LL Cool J and Gloria Gaynor. Will Coss, Macy’s Studios vice president, says the team quickly adjusted plans to deliver the event. The storm forced the first-ever postponement, leaving performers scrambling to extend their stays.
